title: Centrica boss says he is 'hugely concerned' over impact of soaring energy bills
summary: Chris O'Shea says the number of people unable or unwilling to pay their energy bills will increase when prices jump in the new year.
text:
Centrica boss 'hugely concerned' over impact of soaring energy bills
- Published
The boss of British Gas owner Centrica says he is "hugely concerned" about the impact the expected jump in energy bills in January will have on consumers.
Chris O'Shea told the BBC he thought the number of people unable or unwilling to pay their energy bills would rise when prices go up in the new year.
The new energy price cap to take effect from January will be announced on Wednesday and consultancy Cornwall Insight has forecast it will jump by £443 a year for a typical household.
The government has said some households will get £100 to help with energy bills, but Citizens Advice said it was a "drop in the ocean" while one pressure group called for action on "inflated energy firm profits".
Speaking to the Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg programme, O'Shea said the predictions for a "substantial increase" in bills from January were "materially correct", adding that the first quarter of the year was the time when most energy was consumed.
"That's right at the point where people will be paying for Christmas and the like. So I am hugely concerned," he said.
O'Shea added there was a "massive problem" with people not paying their bills in the UK, with some not able to pay their bills and an "increasing number of people that are choosing not to pay their bills".
He said the collective impact of that was that "every single electricity consumer, is paying about £1.50, £1.60 a week to cover the cost of people that are not paying their bills, and it's just going to get worse when bills go up".
The amount owed to energy suppliers by households hit £5bn in the April to June period, according to energy regulator Ofgem.
Wholesale energy prices paid by suppliers have been rising this year as a result of the conflict in the Middle East, which has pushed up bills for households.
Cornwall Insight has predicted Ofgem's energy price cap will rise by 26% to £2,166 a year for a typical household from 1 January.
The price cap affects about 20 million households in England, Scotland and Wales and sets a maximum price for each unit of gas and electricity, so the actual level of bills will vary according to energy usage.
The government has said some households will get a £100 payment to help with energy bills, a policy which was announced in the Budget.
The government has also temporarily cut 5% VAT from electricity bills until the end of June next year, which is expected to save the typical household about £45 a year.
But consumer groups have argued the £100 payment announced in the Budget will not be enough for some.
Citizens Advice said it was a "drop in the ocean" and that we would see "cold-related deaths" this winter.
"For someone in a lot of debt, who can't afford their bills, it's not going to touch the sides."
The Fuel Poverty Action Group said the government and Ofgem needed to take stronger action against energy companies.

title: He expected a small-business loan. He got a 7-year nightmare
summary: America's fastest-growing source of funding for small businesses is also one of the least regulated. One man has waged a long, lonely fight to recoup its punishing cost.
text:
He expected a small-business loan. He got a 7-year nightmare
GLENDALE, Calif. — Sitting at his desk, tucked into a corner of his teenage bedroom — a place where he'd never intended to return, well into middle age — Vahe Shahinian rereads the emails that split his life into before and after.
A broker was offering to fund Shahinian's small business with a line of credit worth $750,000.
It was 2019, and Shahinian's company soared, like a miniature Live Nation-Ticketmaster, selling tickets and producing concerts around Los Angeles and beyond. He imagined how much he could do with stable funding.
The pitch had a catch: Shahinian would first accept a third of the sum and start paying it back immediately, in daily installments of $3,600. After 30 days, he could access the rest of the money. He crunched the numbers, followed up with questions — and took the deal.
Shahinian sent the daily payments, he says, for 30 days. Then 40. Then 50.
The line of credit never came.
"From that day," he says, "it's been one long day, one long nightmare."
For seven years, Shahinian has been mired in the shadowy industry that is now the fastest-growing source of funding for small business in the United States. It's largely unregulated, promising fast money at a tremendous cost. And Shahinian's lawsuit against his funders could become one of the first of its kind to go to trial.
A business in need
Before the "incident," as Shahinian calls his fateful deal, he'd been in business for 15 years, building his company from a side hustle into his main source of income.
Educated as a computer scientist, he'd spent years programming satellites as an aerospace engineer. In 2004, he also developed a site for something he loved in his spare time: community events. Shahinian called his platform for ticketing and seating charts It's My Seat.
Over a decade, Shahinian grew his business from selling tickets to galas and festivals to producing his own shows: booking artists and venues, promoting and marketing. His first concert, by a flamenco guitarist, sold 400 seats. The next, 700. Three years later, 1960s crooner Engelbert Humperdinck performed for 3,000. In 2015, Shahinian expanded again, into touring.
Like most U.S. small businesses, Shahinian says, he self-funded for years. Entrepreneurs like him often dip into savings, family money or home equity; many run up credit cards and reinvest profits.
Shahinian says he had qualified for several generous credit cards, including an American Express with essentially no spending limit. Later, Amex also repeatedly approved him for special merchant financing: instant short-term loans with a low interest rate of 6%.
"All my life," Shahinian offers as his frequent disclaimer these days, "I had never had one missed payment."
By 2018, Shahinian says, he had built his retirement plan: His ticket sales climbed toward $5 million a year, his profits $250,000.

title: Opinion: When should medical school start?
summary: STAT readers weigh in on shortening medical school, fixing pediatric emergency care, and more.
text:
First Opinion is STAT’s platform for interesting, illuminating, and provocative articles about the life sciences writ large, written by biotech insiders, health care workers, researchers, and others.
To encourage robust, good-faith discussion about issues raised in First Opinion essays, STAT publishes selected Letters to the Editor received in response to them. You can submit a Letter to the Editor here, or find the submission form at the end of any First Opinion essay.
The story
“Medical school should start after students take the Step 1 exam,” by Rachel E. Fabi and Amy Caruso Brown
The response
The authors’ proposal hinges on the premise that learning the foundational sciences and learning to become a physician can be separated without compromising either. My first year of medical school was peppered with clinical exposure and taught me otherwise. I floundered with a blood pressure cuff during a wellness visit, fumbled for words as I interviewed a man waiting for a heart transplant, and listened to a patient recount her immense sorrow after multiple miscarriages. These encounters remain among my most formative.
I agree with the authors that students are often preoccupied with medical licensure exams, and that early clinical exposure might not cure this. In my experience, however, it is the strongest counterweight. After meeting those patients, I was learning for more than an exam. The proposed model would abandon that counterweight. Students would still encounter patients eventually, but we would have forfeited valuable time. Becoming a compassionate, humanistic physician is slow work, and it deserves all the time we can offer. A flashcard can teach a student what causes a miscarriage. It takes a patient to teach what it means to grieve one. And that lesson should not wait until after Step 1.
— Surya Pulukuri, Harvard Medical School student
The story
“The economics of the U.S. health care system are broken,” by Paul Markovich
The response
Markovich is correct: The U.S. health care “non-system” is broken. There are many culprits, including hospitals, whose prices are set more by market dominance than by quality. He should also look at the administrative complexity driven largely by our myriad of private insurance companies. Some 25% of U.S. “health care” spending goes to administrative costs. The insurers need to agree on a single set of billing codes and procedures to cut doctors’ and hospitals’ cost of billing. They need to sit down with doctors and come up with a uniform set of procedures needing pre-authorization and a single set of criteria. They need to agree on a small number of policy options that are understandable to the public. Finger-pointing is easy, but should start at home.
— Edward Hoffer, M.D., Harvard Medical School

“Could long-term AI use lead to isolation? We need to find out — but researchers need better access to data,” by Qian Yang, Ned Cooper, and Ibrahim Emara

title: Critics are worried about Anthropic's influence after first day of public trading
summary: Anthropic's initial public offering was a success for shareholders, including its founders. But there were also protests about whether the company can be a responsible steward of AI technology.
text:
Critics are worried about Anthropic's influence after first day of public trading
Anthropic's initial public offering was a success for shareholders, including its founders. But there were also protests about whether the company can be a responsible steward of AI technology.
STEVE INSKEEP, HOST:
Anthropic is now worth $2 trillion, judging by its stock price. The company behind Claude held its initial public offering. It now has a lot of funding to balance the many critics of AI. NPR's Shannon Bond reports.
SHANNON BOND, BYLINE: Inside the Nasdaq stock exchange, Anthropic's executives and co-founders rang the ceremonial bell to open trading on Thursday morning.
(SOUNDBITE OF BELL RINGING)
BOND: Outside in Times Square, a small group of protesters chanted.
(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)
UNIDENTIFIED PROTESTERS: (Chanting) Why you doing IPO? This AI bubble about to blow.
BOND: Activists and AI safety researchers also gathered outside Anthropic's headquarters in downtown San Francisco. They called on the company to slow down the development of advanced AI.
(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)
UNIDENTIFIED ACTIVISTS #1: (Chanting) Please do not accelerate.
UNIDENTIFIED ACTIVISTS #2: (Chanting) Just ask the state to regulate.
BOND: A handful of protesters were arrested in both cities. Anthropic is the first company purely focused on artificial intelligence to go public. And the IPO comes as debates are raging around AI, from the impact of data centers to fears of job losses to worries about AI going rogue. Anthropic itself has fueled some of those fears. It was founded five years ago by a breakaway group of OpenAI employees who were worried that the company wasn't taking safety seriously enough. Before ringing the Nasdaq bell on Thursday, CEO Dario Amodei said Anthropic remains committed to keeping the technology under human control. He said the company won't bend to business or political pressure.
(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)
DARIO AMODEI: If we can show it's possible to make the right choices on safety and still build an incredibly successful company, others in our industry will be inspired to do the same. We call this a race to the top.
BOND: Amodei and his six co-founders each made about $280 million selling shares in this week's IPO. They each hold a stake in the company worth about $23 billion at Thursday's closing price.
Shannon Bond, NPR News.
INSKEEP: And we'll note that Anthropic is a financial supporter of NPR.
(SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC)

title: Opinion: How Kennedy and MAHA could help stop measles
summary: Kennedy and MAHA say they aren’t anti-vaccine. They can prove it by promoting the MMR vaccine, writes Brinda Adhikari.
text:
A version of this article first appeared on the Substack of “Why Should I Trust You?”
On Tuesday, after the United States lost its measles elimination status, health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. posted on X that he wanted to stop measles from spreading in America. “We will stop measles outbreaks, protect American families, and work to regain U.S. measles elimination status. I continue to recommend [measles, mumps, and rubella] vaccination as the most effective way to prevent measles.”
Well, Secretary Kennedy, do I have an idea for you …
It involves mobilizing a movement you helped build, a movement that has successfully organized millions of Americans around issues related to their health. I’m talking about MAHA.
Right now, the discourse is playing out like this: Medical societies are expressing alarm over the loss of measles elimination status, while many politicians blame Kennedy and the Trump administration for failing to adequately respond.
Kennedy’s defenders clap back by reminding us that other countries have lost elimination status in recent years, too, that these are all efforts to undermine Kennedy and that his administration is doing what it can.
I understand on some level that, as a society, we need to litigate what went wrong. But candidly, I’m much more interested in something else: Who might be best positioned to reach the Americans that public health officials are struggling to persuade to get the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine?
What I learned from listening
I’ll start by saying that I believe in the measles vaccine. I was vaccinated as a child. I’ve vaccinated my two kids. I don’t identify as particularly vaccine skeptical. I’ve sometimes wondered why we have so many vaccine recommendations in this country compared with others, but I generally trust my doctors and haven’t (yet) experienced any major adverse reactions that might have led me to question that trust.
Over the last two years of making the podcast “Why Should I Trust You?,” my co-hosts and I have had the privilege of speaking with many people who feel quite differently than I do about vaccines, public health, and the medical system, and what they see as blind faith in expertise.
I’ve learned a tremendous amount. These conversations have made me question my own assumptions and better understand why I trust institutions, while sometimes realizing that I, too, harbor mistrust. While some of these conversations have been with people who are unwaveringly anti-vaccine, most have been with people who have taken some vaccines and harbor doubts about others.
They’ve also given me a front-row seat to something else: the MAHA grassroots movement’s astonishing ability to organize.

title: MP criticises Guernsey and Jersey company ownership register plans
summary: Sir Andrew Mitchell says access should be easier for people tackling financial crime.
text:
MP criticises company ownership register plans
- Published
Plans to improve transparency over company ownership in Guernsey and Jersey have come under criticism from a Westminster MP, who says they "do not go nearly far enough".
The comments come after Guernsey, external and Jersey, external set out plans to allow approved applicants access to information about who owns or controls companies when investigating suspected financial crime.
Sir Andrew Mitchell, who has campaigned for greater scrutiny of company ownership, said there were "immediate indications" the proposals would fall short.
He said limits on access to the information could mean "national security threats may remain entirely invisible to investigators".
The plans follow a joint commitment made by Guernsey, Jersey and the Isle of Man in December 2023 to increase transparency around company ownership and help tackle money laundering, terrorist financing and other financial crime.
Currently, information about who ultimately owns or controls companies is generally only available to law enforcement agencies, regulators and certain regulated businesses carrying out anti-money laundering checks.
The new proposals would allow journalists, academics and other applicants with a legitimate interest to apply for access.
'Defeats the object'
Sir Andrew said investigators could face a "catch-22" because they may need access to the register to prove wrongdoing in the first place.
He also said he understood applicants would have to show they had been unable to find the information elsewhere, arguing: "This entirely defeats the object of a register."
Jersey's consultation response says applicants would be expected to show that "all reasonable alternative sources have been exhausted" before access was granted.
Guernsey's published response does not explicitly set out the same requirement.
He said: "Access should be open to those from other jurisdictions, for example those in the global south from whom much of the world's dirty money was stolen in the first place."
Sir Andrew also questioned whether users would have to pay to access the information, saying: "This information should be free at the point of access."
He said the proposals should eventually lead to fully public registers.
'Effective transparency framework'
Both the governments of Guernsey and Jersey rejected Sir Andrew's criticism and said they continue to meet international standards in tackling financial crime.
A Government of Jersey spokesperson said the concerns raised by him "do not accurately reflect what is in Jersey's consultation response paper".
They said the policy was intended to help Jersey meet its international commitments while maintaining "a fair, proportionate, and effective transparency framework".
They added: "Jersey continues to meet international standards for transparency and countering money laundering, terrorist financing and proliferation financing."

title: STAT+: Is MAHA’s think tank in the tank? Tax filings show low reserves
summary: Tax filings show the MAHA Institute spent more than $1 million in 2025, ending its first year with just $171,000 as events and overhead drained its cash.
text:
WASHINGTON —The MAHA Institute, a nonprofit “think tank” launched to support Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s health agenda, burned over $1 million in 2025, leaving it with little cash on hand to continue operating, tax documents obtained by STAT show.
The group started 2025 with nearly $1.3 million in its coffers, but ended the year with just $171,000, per its latest IRS return, filed this week. That 86% drop was hardly offset by the group’s revenue, which was just shy of $67,000 for the year.
“To have lost over $1 million is pretty notable to me,” said Brian Mittendorf, a professor at Ohio State University who specializes in nonprofit accounting.

title: Italian jeweller and businessman Paolo Bulgari dies aged 89
summary: In a statement to Italian media, his family remember him as "the greatest jeweller of our time".
text:
Italian jeweller and businessman Paolo Bulgari dies aged 89
- Published
Italian jeweller Paolo Bulgari, who helped turn his family's business into a global luxury brand, has died in Rome aged age 89.
His family announced the news, remembering him as "the greatest jeweller of our time", according to Italian media.
Paolo Bulgari was Chairman of the Bvlgari Group since 1984 and its jewellery pieces have adorned Hollywood stars and royalty including Diana, Princess of Wales.
The company Bvlgari posted an online tribute to the "true creative soul", whose work would "continue to inspire generations to come".
The firm, Bulgari, was set up by his grandfather, Greek silversmith Sotirios Voulgaris, in Rome in the late 19th century - who later adapted his name to Bulgari in Italian.
Originally from Paramythia, a mountain village in the Epirus region of northwestern Greece renowned for its silver jewellery, Voulgaris fled Ottoman rule and settled in Naples before opening a shop in Rome.
Paolo Bulgari joined the company shortly after leaving school, becoming an expert in gemstones - eventually leading the business and overseeing international growth.
The Bulgari family favoured bold gemstones, rich yellow gold, generous proportions and unexpected colour combinations to set them apart from the delicate asethetic associated with Parisian jewellery houses.
The business broke into luxury markets and diversified beyond jewellery into watches, perfumes, leather goods and hotels.
"Paolo Bulgari began collaborating with his father in 1960, specialising in the knowledge of precious stones, of which he was one of the world's leading experts, and refining the sensibility and aesthetic sense that are at the root of the Bvlgari style," the Bvlgari company posted on social media., external
"He poured his heart into his craft and into nurturing the talents of young designers, leaving an indelible mark on the world of jewellery.
"Thank you, Mr. Paolo, your legacy as a brilliant beacon of creative inspiration will continue to inspire generations to come."
The post included a quote from Paolo Bulgari: "Everything can be a source of inspiration. There are no rules in creativity. Never."
The designer brand's celebrity clients have included Elizabeth Taylor, Audrey Hepburn, Marilyn Monroe, Ingrid Bergman, Sophie Loren, Anne Hathaway, Zendaya and Rihanna.
In 2011 the family sold its controlling stake to the French luxury group LVMH, in a deal worth about 3.7 billion euros.
In 2019, he and his wife established the Paolo Bulgari Foundation to support young people through schooling and job training in disadvantaged neighbourhoods on the outskirts of Rome.
The funeral will take place in Rome on Monday, 23 November in the Basilica of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme.
  - Published7 March 2011

title: Employers are being asked to give interview feedback - here's what applicants want
summary: People say they often hear nothing back after applying for jobs. But could employers be forced to respond to every applicant?
text:
Employers are being asked to give interview feedback - here's what applicants want
- Published
Have you ever applied for a job or attended an interview, only to hear absolutely nothing back from the employer?
So-called "job ghosting" has become a big problem for jobseekers in the UK, leaving them "demoralised", denting their confidence and undermining their hopes of finding work.
It's an issue that was mentioned in former minister Alan Milburn's major review into young people who are not in employment, education or training - those dubbed as Neets - this week.
Among his recommendations - aimed at reducing the proportion of Neets from 13% to about 5% by 2036 - Milburn proposed that large employers should give all unsuccessful job applicants under 25 "meaningful feedback".
The report's proposals relate mostly to England, with a recommendation that Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland adapt the principles to suit their own systems.
But is feedback for all applicants realistic, given the vast number of applications these firms receive? And what can people do to improve their chances in such a tough job market?
Yugraj Samrai, 23, from Coventry is currently unemployed and says he has submitted hundreds of job applications since he graduated from his marketing degree in July.
But 30 to 40% of the time he hears nothing back at all, which can make him "feel like a statistic, not a person".
He tells the BBC: "I understand there are very few graduate jobs available, but at least give me a response to say whether I'll progress onto the next stage or not."
'I'm just not hearing anything'
Ffion Johns, from Llanelli, has been unemployed since June and did not get an interview until September after submitting 70 applications.
The 24-year-old says her biggest problem throughout the job-hunting process has been the lack of feedback about why she didn't get the job, so she knows what to fix next time.
Sometimes she has even been ghosted after attending an interview.
"With most of these roles I'm not getting a rejection. I'm just not hearing anything, which can be quite frustrating," she says.
Research by head-hunting firm Robert Walters last year found 86% of UK job hunters said their applications had been ignored, with no response at all from the hiring organisation.
The Milburn report, external says this "wall of silence" is especially hard on young people as it gives them "nothing to learn from". It adds that "time and emotional investment" goes into their applications.
"It can really take hours and hours, so it just feels even worse to not even have that be recognised," says Jessica Anderson, 21, from Swindon.
Employers say they are being flooded with job applications in a very competitive jobs market and it can be hard to respond to all of them.
And AI is adding to the problem, enabling applicants to submit large numbers of applications in the hope of improving their chances.

title: STAT+: Pharmalittle: We’re reading about Sanofi eyeing Insmed, AI speeding drug development, and more
summary: Sanofi weighs an Insmed takeover, the FDA slams J&J over misleading bladder cancer drug claims, and more pharma news:
text:
And so, another working week will soon draw to a close. Not a moment too soon, yes? This is, you may recall, our treasured signal to daydream about weekend plans. Our agenda is, so far, rather modest. We plan to catch up on our reading, escort Mrs. Pharmalot to a musical event, and promenade with the official mascot. We also plan to hold another listening party, where the rotation will likely include this, this, this, this and this. And what about you? As noted previously, this remains a fine time to enjoy the great outdoors — perhaps a drive in the country is in order or a long walk by a lake or ocean. If the weather fails to cooperate, you could take in a moving picture show. Or maybe this is an opportunity to boost your local economy with a holiday purchase. Speaking of holidays, we will be off next week but never fear, a team of pinch hitters will be on hand. Meanwhile, whatever you do over the next 10 days or so, we hope you do something smashing. But be safe. Enjoy, and see you soon…
Artificial intelligence has sped early-stage drug development work at some of the world’s largest pharmaceutical companies this year, cutting by as much as half the time it takes to produce new molecules and move them into the clinic, Reuters explains. The top scientists at Bristol Myers Squibb, Novartis, Eli Lilly, Sanofi, Novo Nordisk and AstraZeneca all say they have moved beyond less glamorous tasks for AI like preparing regulatory filings. They are now using the technology for designing molecules, sorting out the most promising ones, and identifying safety risks.
A few of the largest pharmaceutical companies have told a Congressional committee that they do not plan to start new clinical trial sites in the Xinjiang region of China or at hospitals affiliated with the Chinese military, STAT writes. The disclosure was made by the House Select Committee on China, which last June opened investigations into five companies — Merck, Eli Lilly, AbbVie, Pfizer, and Bristol Myers Squibb — over concerns about intellectual property exposure, military entanglements, and ethical standards at trial sites in sensitive regions of the country.

title: Can AI really help spot Black Friday deals? We put it to the test
summary: We put four AI models to the test to see if they could save us money on a new TV.
text:
Can AI really help spot Black Friday deals? We put it to the test
- Published
Whether it's scrolling through endless choice, spotting fake reviews, or working out if a "deal" is a deal at all, Black Friday sums up a lot of online woes.
Retailers promise bargains - but the sheer number of offers can leave us feeling no closer to finding the best deal.
It's an area where generative AI products, such as ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini, have promised to help.
But are they any good at finding Black Friday deals? We had a go ourselves a week ahead of the big day.
Figures suggest relatively few UK shoppers currently go to AI tools for help.
A recent YouGov survey of 19 countries found the UK ranked second-last in the proportion of people who said they had used AI to help them shop.
Crucially, 36% of respondents who said they would be shopping around Black Friday didn't plan to use an AI tool at all.
But the survey suggested a growing number of people were considering it - and tech firms have released features to capitalise on this.
Amazon launched Alexa for Shopping for UK users in November and OpenAI launched a Shopping Research tool on ChatGPT days before last year's Black Friday.
In the US, Google recently launched Universal Cart, with AI-powered features such as price tracking and identification of relevant promo codes.
But there has been criticism that fact-checking AI ends up taking more time, while some brands are working to try to make sure their products show up in chatbot answers.
We asked four models to find a 55-inch TV deal, using the free versions of many of the most popular tools.
While this was not a rigorous scientific test, the experience we had produced mixed results.
ChatGPT - full price and not available to buy
OpenAI's ChatGPT came up with four options.
Its top pick was a Hisense TV on Chinese retailer Joybuy's website, on sale for £499 down from £649.
The next recommendation was a 55-inch TCL-branded TV, but a sidebar showed prices for the 50-inch version, from £379 to £814.
Option three was the same Hisense TV as before, but for full price at £649 from John Lewis and Richer Sounds.
This was the "best safer purchase" according to ChatGPT, as the sites offered longer guarantee periods.
But clicking on the links did not go well. Both retailers said the TV was no longer listed online.
The fourth option was equally fruitless - another TCL TV, at full price, £150 over our budget and not available online.
At the bottom, ChatGPT served one last offer - "one OLED option to compare" - for a £1,100 LG TV that was marked as "Ad".
Claude - honest, but not too helpful
Claude produced the shortest answer of all the models we tested, and unlike the others, it did not give much detail on the specifications of each model.
Instead, it seemed to base its results on a small number of reviews published online.
It recommended the same two TCL TVs as ChatGPT.
But when we clicked on the links, they sent us to two dead pages on the Richer Sounds website.

title: Tech stock sell-off drags markets down as Anthropic shares slide
summary: Pressures weighed on US markets, with the S&P 500 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average pushed into correction territory.
text:
Tech stock sell-off drags markets down as Anthropic shares slide
- Published
Anthropic's shares have dropped back towards their initial price after a soaring first day on the stock market, as a wider tech sell-off dragged markets down.
The sell-off comes as concerns remain over the speed and size of artificial intelligence investment, but also as some large companies including Nvidia and SpaceX faced specific issues that worried investors.
Those pressures combined to weigh on US markets through Friday, with all key US indexes closing sharply down on the day, furthering earlier falls over the week.
Both the S&P 500 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average were pushed into correction territory, a point where they are trading at 10% or more down from a recent high.
The S&P 500 closed down 3.7%, the Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 1.9% and the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index plunged 5.3%. However, all three indexes were up on where they were a year ago.
The speed at which AI investment has been growing - with more than $1 trillion spent in the last year alone by a small handful of major tech companies - has led to ongoing concerns of a financial bubble. Questions are being raised over whether those investments will pay off, and when.
Investors were also spooked after the Democrats' resounding win in the US midterms in early November, which sparked fears of a reduction in AI development.
Despite a positive first day of trading, Anthropic's shares fell on Friday, dropping at one point by more than 12% to about $85, close to its initial public offering (IPO) price of $83. It closed down 8.5%, reversing half of the gains made on Thursday.
The artificial intelligence (AI) company's introduction to the Nasdaq stock exchange on Thursday was a crucial test for the industry and was largely seen as a success, with trading starting at $111.50 before easing to end the day up 17% at $97.17.
Analysts said volatility was to be expected in the first days or even weeks of Anthropic's trading, as the company was the first frontier AI firm to go public so had no direct peers.
Some have also noted the similarities with Elon Musk's SpaceX, which at the time of its debut in June was the largest IPO on record. Shares in the rocket and AI company experienced large swings in its first few weeks of trading.
Ed Moya, a strategist at market intelligence firm AlphaSense, said Anthropic's blockbuster IPO did not appear to have restored confidence in the broader AI market.
While AI demand was still very strong, Moya told the BBC that investors were trying to answer the question of how much were they willing to pay for that growth.
"As we've gone through the past past few weeks, it seems that there's been more risks that have surfaced," he said.
"Right now you're starting to see Wall Street is trying to shift from rewarding growth at any price, to demanding stronger cash flow and a clearer path to profitability."

Which, speaking of …
Peptides go mainstream
Unapproved and off-label peptide drugs have long been popular with bodybuilders looking for an edge, but they could soon become a mass market health product, thanks to new initiatives from two popular telehealth companies.
Hims & Hers unveiled Thursday its Peptides+ program, offering two peptides alongside several compounded medications popular among peptide users. Noom announced its own offerings this week as well. This follows a decision by FDA leaders to — despite the concerns of staff scientists – allow compounders to produce six peptides that haven’t been approved by the agency, including BPC-157 and TB-500. Hims said it will soon offer BPC-157 and TB-500; Noom is considering adding them too.
Telehealth companies argue their peptides will be safer and more reliable than the black market “research-grade” products often used today, and Hims notes its program will offer twice-yearly blood tests for patient monitoring. But critics contend selling drugs that haven’t gone through the FDA’s approval process for their proposed use will bring products that have not been proven safe or effective to many patients who would not have otherwise encountered them.

U.S. drugmakers pull back from (parts of) China
A few of the largest U.S. drugmakers recently told a Congressional committee they would not start new clinical trials in the Xinjiang region of China or in hospitals affiliated with the Chinese military.
The concessions come as U.S. pharmas rush to partner with Chinese biotech startups and hospitals, alarming some American lawmakers. Last year, the House Select Committee on China opened investigations into Merck, Eli Lilly, AbbVie, Pfizer, and Bristol Myers Squibb over concerns about intellectual property exposure, military entanglements, and ethical standards at trial sites. All five of those companies have now agreed to not start any new trials at hospitals with ties to the People’s Liberation Army.
Four — all but AbbVie — agreed to stop trials in Xinjiang, where the Chinese government has targeted Uyghurs and other ethnic and religious minorities. title: Faisal Islam: This cost-cutting UK-EU deal doesn't mean lower prices will follow
summary: The trade deal is unlikely lower food prices for shoppers, but should boost the economy more than other post-Brexit agreements.
text:
Faisal Islam: This cost-cutting UK-EU deal doesn't mean lower prices will follow
- Published
The prime minister made a lot of the UK's new deal with the EU cutting costs for business and consumers during tough times.
In another world, Andy Burnham would have loved for the nation's supermarkets to clearly announce that they could cut food prices as a result of this latest agreement on food exports.
And while grocers have very much welcomed Friday's announcement, they have notably not committed to price cuts as a direct result of this move.
The managing director of M&S, Alex Freudmann, called the deal a "major step forward", saying it would remove bureaucracy. Tesco chief executive Ken Murphy added it was "good news for British farmers and producers".
Freudmann highlighted some of hoops that were hurting UK-EU trade, using the example that "getting our spaghetti Bolognese from Lincolnshire onto a shelf in Dublin takes hundreds of extra miles, mountains of paperwork, a vet's signature and even the Latin name of a cow".
Such measures will no longer need to be taken once this deal kicks in. Good news for business exports then, but will that lead to lower shopping bills here in the UK?
This deal will matter for food exporters - it may not have a clear visible impact at the checkout.
Privately, industry insiders say there are too many moving parts in the world economy, especially given the energy price shock resulting from war in the Middle East.
It is more a hope than will at this stage. The industry and government hope that the reduction in costs for food producers and sellers will be passed on to customers.
This is not the first time Labour has sought to reduce the weekly shop costs. Sir Keir Starmer's administration floated the idea that supermarkets might even offer some form of branded discounts, a suggestion that was met with collective bemusement by those in the industry.
However, there will be less paperwork, checks and red tape on food imports too, but they were already lightly enforced.
No longer will hundreds of pages of documents be required. No longer will perishable goods lose valuable hours or days at border checks. No longer will the incorrect colour of ink or Latin name for a meat disallow a shipment of British exports.
Some, though not all of the 24% hit since 2019 to the real value of agrifood exports, could be regained by a bonfire of this red tape.
In particular, smaller exporters of food will be able to return to the large EU market.
But the extra benefit here is unclear, and there could be extra checks and costs required instead on non-EU food imports.
The government's own assessment is that the economy will gain £5bn through this, or 0.14% by 2040.
Critics point out that this benefit does not include the quid pro quo - having to align with EU laws. Farmers have pointed to compliance with pesticides and fungicide regulation.

title: Patients have little say in how brain implant trials are done. Ian Burkhart wants to change that
summary: Ian Burkhart, founder of a coalition of brain implant trial participants, says device developers should give patients more agency in research.
text:
So you’ve been diagnosed with ALS — what now? Maybe you join a clinical trial for a brain implant that could help you do things like move your hand or talk to your loved ones. But can you influence the research as a participant? And what happens to the data collected from your brain when the study ends?
A new report addresses these and other questions, exploring how trials of implanted brain-computer interfaces can better address the interests and concerns of participants, who often join in a last-ditch attempt to improve their communication, mobility, or autonomy.
Published by the BCI Pioneers Coalition last week, the report outlines 13 recommendations for startups, researchers, and regulators on managing post-trial care, informed consent, and neural data privacy.
“These studies can sometimes last years, and it becomes a big part of someone’s life. You want there to be as much agency from the participant as possible,” said Ian Burkhart, who co-founded the coalition, with other participants in early studies of implantable BCI devices, to share patient feedback with developers and researchers. Burkhart said the report emerged out of discussions between him and other study participants, who felt they had very little say in how trials were conducted.
The recommendations arrive as the field moves from a niche, proof-of-concept phase into a humming neurotechnology startup ecosystem with eager investors and multiple clinical trials testing implanted devices’ safety and efficacy. Ethicist Anna Wexler believes that scientists need better policies to ensure participants’ rights and autonomy.
“There is no good solution right now. We talk about potentially mandatory insurance policies, escrows, and institutions committing support, but right now we just don’t actually have solutions,” Wexler, a University of Pennsylvania Perelman School of Medicine professor, said during a panel at a recent brain-computer interface industry conference in New York.
STAT spoke with Burkhart about his own experiences as someone with tetraplegia and as a former BCI user shopping around for his next device. He wants to make sure that during his next trial, he has more clarity around the study’s overall expectations, what he can do with the data generated, and what will happen to his care after he is explanted.
You were implanted in 2014 with a device at Ohio State University that helped you move your arm. What happened when the study ended?
When our study was starting to wind down because of some funding issues, the institutional review board said, “Well, we can just have them have the device taken out, and then if it gets funded again, they can just put another one back in.” Like, that’s great when it’s not you that’s going through experimental brain surgery.
